name: Doorway pec stretch
lead: The doorway pec stretch is a simple chest-opening stretch: the forearm or hand rests on a door frame and the body leans or steps forward, lengthening the pectoral muscles at the front of the chest. People use it to loosen a tight chest and ease the rounded-shoulder look, so the shoulders sit more open and the chest appears broader and more upright.

The pectoralis major is a fan-shaped muscle that flexes, adducts and internally rotates the upper arm and draws the shoulder blade forward and down [1]. General descriptions of posture note that tight pectoral muscles together with weaker upper-back and abdominal muscles can affect how a person stands [2]. Lifters in training logs on T Nation mention pec stretches as part of warm-ups and mobility sessions alongside face pulls, hangs and hip-flexor work [3][4].

chain: Shoulders can settle back and open
angle.text: People use the stretch to counter a hunched, rounded-shoulder look, aiming for an open chest and squarer shoulders. It is commonly paired with upper-back work such as rows and face pulls.

paras: The usual form places a forearm vertically on a door frame with the elbow near shoulder height, then a step forward through the doorway turns the chest away from the arm. Variations change the arm height to emphasise different parts of the chest, and some people use a wall, a corner, a rack or a resistance band instead [5]. Lifters also describe weighted and ring-based pec stretches in their logs [4].

In appearance-focused communities the stretch sits in the posture toolkit: loosen the chest, strengthen the upper back, and the shoulders look more open. Training-log posts show it used as a warm-up between sets and on mobility days, and some lifters write that a good pec stretch gives them a pump in the shoulders [3][5]. Others use it after returning from shoulder injury to regain overhead range [6]. Discussion of long-muscle-length training also appears, where lifters note that working in a stretched position is linked to muscle growth [7].

lore.intro: The stretch comes up in lifting forums as routine mobility work rather than a headline technique [3][5].

claims.claim: Stretching the chest opens up rounded shoulders
claims.believers: Lifters describe feeling looser and standing more upright after pec stretching combined with back work [4][5].
claims.experts: Posture overviews note that tight pectorals and weaker back and core muscles can affect posture [2]. No study cited here tests the doorway stretch specifically for appearance.

claims.claim: A pec stretch before pressing improves the feel of chest work
claims.believers: Training logs describe better chest and shoulder sensation after stretching [3].
claims.experts: Discussions of long-muscle-length training note a link between stretched positions and muscle gain, though that concerns loaded training rather than warm-up stretches [7].

card.summary: A door-frame chest stretch people use to open tight pecs and sit with more open, upright shoulders.
card.aka: Door frame chest stretch, wall pec stretch
card.note: Stretch gently; sharp pain in the shoulder or chest is a reason to stop.

quick.overview:
The doorway pec stretch lengthens the muscles at the front of the chest by leaning through a door frame with the forearm braced on it. It needs no equipment and takes under a minute.

People use it to loosen a tight chest and help the shoulders sit back, which can make posture look more open and the upper body more upright.
quick.mechanism: The arm is fixed against the frame so that stepping forward pulls the pectoral muscle and front shoulder into a lengthened position. Lifters usually pair it with upper-back exercises.
quick.risks: Over-stretching the front of the shoulder can cause discomfort, and people with shoulder instability or prior labrum surgery are often cautious about how far they go. Product-free and low risk otherwise.
